title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Nestor Caticha, João Henrique Sant'Ana, Felippe Alves, Davi Bastos Costa, Mariana Mercucci, Juan P. Neirotti, Otavio Citton, Renato Vicente
abstract: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.
summary: This work models opinion formation and discrimination in multi-agent systems using adaptive learning rules. By introducing a structural group bias, the authors derive a phase diagram showing four distinct collective states. The findings demonstrate that simple local interactions can generate complex, measurable forms of societal polarization.
main_problem: The paper theoretically investigates how polarization and discrimination emerge in a population of learning agents through repeated pairwise interactions.
main_result: The dynamics generate a rich phase diagram in the bias parameter space, revealing four distinct collective states, including spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism.
method: The study uses online Bayesian rules derived from teacher-student learning to model adaptive updates to opinion weights and trust estimates.
model_or_system: The model consists of N agents interacting over P issues, where agents maintain linear decision layers for binary opinions and evolving trust estimates for every other agent.
key_observables: Order parameters characterizing pairwise opinion alignment, trust, and group membership.
important_parameters: Bias strength ($b$) and prevalence ($f_b$) of group bias.
main_assumptions: Agents use adaptive linear decision layers, and the analysis relies on order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect local dynamics to collective states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the phase diagram in the $(b, f_b)$ space, illustrating the four collective states. Other figures detail the evolution of opinion and trust profiles.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the local learning dynamics via Bayesian updates, then introduces group bias, and finally uses order parameters to map the local dynamics onto a global phase diagram.
why_interesting: The use of order parameters and phase diagrams to characterize emergent collective behavior in a system governed by local, adaptive learning rules mirrors concepts used in spin-glass physics and complex systems modeling.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Left: the phase diagram in the space of bias strength b and the fraction fb of biased agents, obtained from societies of N = 100 agents by averaging two realizations at each point of a 300 × 300 grid. In (I) out-group favoritism leads to a frustrated, in the sense of spin glass, structure of trust relations and opinions. In (II), polarization, opinion and trust form two camps unrelated to class. In (IIIa), both trust and opinion are highly correlated with class; in (IIIb), b is so high that irrespective of opinion, trust and class are correlated. Figure 2: Evidence landscape and modulation functions. Left: Minus the log-evidence −ln Z. Online SGD follows its negative gradient toward higher-evidence regions and away from the dis- sonant configurations where evidence is low. Center and right: the opinion and trust modulation functions, Fw and Fµ. Learning and unlearning occurs in the low evidence regions which represent cognitive dissonance, i.e. when the emitter agrees (respect. disagrees) with a receiver that it distrusts (respect. trusts). Figure 3: Opinion and trust updates under in-context learning. The backgrounds show the analytic functions and the points show the measured changes divided by one global fitted scale for each experiment. The opinion experiment (left) contains 550 measured changes, with 94.7% sign agreement and rank correlation rs = 0.90. The trust experiment (right) contains 712 measured changes, with 86.0% sign agreement and correlation r = 0.85.
